items.title: 489 Spear Points Show Clovis Newcomers Wasted Less Stone
items.abstract: In Tennessee’s chert-rich river valley, the first Ice Age hunters resharpened their points to stubs while Cumberland successors discarded usable ones. In the Tennessee River Valley, countless small drainages have cut down into four chert-bearing rock formations, the Fort Payne, the Warsaw, the St. Louis and the Ste. Genevieve, and left the stone lying in tabular slabs and cobbles along their beds. Chert breaks like thick glass, and it is the stone Ice Age knappers in the region worked into spear points. The two archaeologists behind a new study of the valley’s earliest artifacts describe its supply as effectively limitless, which makes it odd that the first people known to have lived there, the makers of Clovis points, used it as though it might run out. Jesse Tune, director of the Center for Archaeological Research, examines a replica of a Cumberland spear point, one of two types of stone projectiles he and Shane Miller, assistant professor of anthropology at the University of Alabama, studied to gain insights into the lives of ancient inhabitants of the Tennessee River Valley. items.title: Teotihuacan Writing Was Real: 3 Glyphs on a Mexican Cliff
items.abstract: Red glyphs painted in Cave 19 at Chalcatzingo, Morelos, name a Singing Mountain and add new evidence that Teotihuacan had a true writing system. On the western face of Cerro Delgado, a 110-metre hill of volcanic rock in the Mexican state of Morelos, there is a rock shelter that nobody can walk to anymore. The team that recorded it in August 2022 climbed the hill from its gentler eastern side and abseiled down the cliff, and they suspect that in antiquity people reached it from below on scaffold-like ladders, using footholds that someone chipped into the steeper stretches of rock. Archaeologists call it Cave 19, though it barely qualifies as a cave: it is 5.43 metres wide and at most 2.24 metres deep, and the lip of rock overhead hangs between 1.46 and 1.85 metres above the floor, low enough that a tall visitor stoops. At the back, above a bedrock shelf blackened by old fire, someone sometime between the fourth and sixth centuries AD took a brush and dark red pigment, probably haematite, and painted three designs. WARSAW, POLAND—According to a Phys.org report, a 400-year-old shipwreck has been discovered in northern Germany’s Bay of Greifswald. The remnants of the vessel were identified in 2023 during work to prepare for the construction of an underwater gas pipeline. A rescue team of five archaeologists, including Michał Grabowski of the University of Warsaw, completed 22 dives over 12 days to recover as much as possible from the wreckage, which rested in heavy silt under 25 feet of water. Fragments of the ship’s hull showed that it had been made with planks held together with iron nails and a mix of tar and animal hair. Tree-ring analysis of one of the timbers revealed that the tree had been cut down between 1626 and 1639. In all, archaeologists recovered shoe soles, a stitched leather strap, pulley blocks, an anchor, rope, barrel staves, and a hollowed-out oak trunk that may have been used as the ship’s bilge pump. items.title: How Henry VII seized – and kept – the crown
items.abstract: Sean Cunningham reassesses the first Tudor king's critical reputation, exploring the delicate balancing act that defined his reign Henry VII is often remembered as a cold, calculating and penny-pinching monarch whose relentless pursuit of an ever-tightening grip on the throne overshadowed his achievements. But how fair is that reputation? And what can the real history behind this popular perception tell us about the challenges, anxieties and realities of Henry's kingship? items.title: Affaire de la bactérie tueuse dans l'Aisne: six bouchers mis en examen
items.abstract: Plus d’un an après la vague d’intoxications à Escherichia coli qui avait touché 32 personnes dans l’Aisne et provoqué la mort d’une fillette de 11 ans, l’enquête connaît un nouveau tournant : six bouchers viennent d’être mis en examen. Derrière ce dossier judiciaire se trouve une bactérie dont certaines souches, productrices de shigatoxines, peuvent provoquer chez l’enfant une complication potentiellement mortelle, le syndrome hémolytique et urémique (SHU).

items.title: Robot wars in the classroom: why AI in education is nothing new
items.abstract: As the role of AI in education sparks debate, Laura Tisdall examines past technological advances in teaching, and how they were received at the time In 1929, the British magazine Teachers World identified ‘A Possible Menace to the Free Development of Education’. The putative culprit was BBC Radio, which had begun its schools broadcasting programme five years earlier, provoking fears that teachers would simply become ‘machine minders’. Such concerns pre-dated radios, though. The first ‘teaching machines’ were developed in the US in the 19th century; it was claimed that they could, for example, teach students to spell by getting them to turn a crank to arrange letters in the correct order. Panic reached fever pitch by the 1960s, when new electronic ‘automatic teachers’ emerged, popularised by the American psychologist BF Skinner. More widely, commentators ranging from Canadian radical feminist Shulamith Firestone (in The Dialectic of Sex , 1970) to US businessman Alvin Toffler ( Future Shock , 1970) predicted that humanoid robots would soon be indistinguishable from real people. items.title: Hitler ordered my father’s death – but an SS general spared his life
items.abstract: When he was captured by the Nazis in 1944, George Lascelles – the eldest nephew of King George VI – became one of Colditz Castle’s most important prisoners. David Lascelles tells the remarkable story behind his father’s time in captivity, and why, decades later, he decided to track down a pistol belonging to the man who let his father walk free It was April 1945. As the Second World War entered its final stages, my father, First Lieutenant George Lascelles of the Grenadier Guards, was imprisoned in Oflag IV-C, Colditz Castle . The prisoners there called it a straflager – a punishment camp – much to the irritation of their German captors, who insisted it was just an ordinary PoW camp but with better security. It was where they sent particularly troublesome prisoners, the habitual escapers and those considered to be deutschfeindlich , hostile to German ways. My father, just 22 years old, didn’t see himself as any of those. He had been a prisoner for less than a year and had never tried to escape. What he was, though, was well connected. His maternal uncle was King George VI , and he was one of a small group of young British officers being held together in Colditz, all of them related…

items.title: Göbeklitepe’s 928 Bone Fragments May Be Landslide Debris
items.abstract: The site’s first intact burials suggest much of its scattered human bone began in graves under house floors, not in the rites of a Neolithic skull cult. On the southeastern side of the mound at Göbeklitepe, workers digging a drainage channel in 2017 for the site’s new protective shelter came down on a pit cut into the plaster floor of a rectangular building, the first intact grave anyone had excavated at a place most of the world knows as a temple. The pit was roughly kidney-shaped and held the bones of at least three people, and those bones had been moved around inside it: the skulls gathered in the southeastern corner, most of the rest piled toward the middle, several long bones laid along the western wall. Göbeklitepe (the older two-word spelling, Göbekli Tepe, is still the more common one in English) lies 15 kilometers northeast of the city of Şanlıurfa in southeastern Türkiye, and for the first two decades after excavation began in 1995 it was described as a sanctuary: a place where hunter-gatherers came together to raise T-shaped pillars carved with wild animals, and where hardly anyone lived. items.title: Are these history's greatest losers? 19 people who had glory snatched away from them
items.abstract: History may celebrate the winners, but what about those who came tantalisingly close to the top spot? Jonny Wilkes shines a light on 19 famous ‘almosts’ At the 2026 London Marathon, Kenya’s Sabastian Sawe made history by becoming the first runner ever to finish the 26.2 miles in under two hours, breaking the tape with a time of 1:59:30. While the crowd cheered and the commentators tried to capture the significance of the moment, another runner, Yomif Kejelcha of Ethiopia, quietly passed the finish line too, and also under two hours. While still a remarkable achievement, it is doomed to be overshadowed by Sawe – and all for the sake of 11 seconds. Second place, the silver medal, the so-called ‘first loser’: it can be a heartbreaking position, to be so close and yet so far from the ultimate glory. (Before you feel too bad for Kejelcha, though, it is worth noting that this was his first-ever marathon, so imagine what he could accomplish with more training.) Whether in the field of exploration, invention, politics or sport, history is replete with examples of close-but-no-cigar runners-up, although their names don’t fill as much space in the history books as the ones who pipped them. items.title: 1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
items.abstract: Scientists studying ancient Australian rocks uncovered more than 12,000 fossils from some of the oldest known eukaryotes on Earth. These early complex cells lived in settings ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea, but only where oxygen was available. Oxygen-free environments contained simpler microbes instead. The findings strengthen the idea that oxygen played a crucial role in the emergence of complex life.

items.title: Isotopes Flag Just 17 of 199 as Migrants in Bronze Age Greece
items.abstract: Strontium isotope analysis of six Greek sites puts migrants at 5 to 10 percent across the Bronze Age, with young adults the likeliest newcomers. On the summit of Mount Kynortion, above the slope near Epidavros where a sanctuary of Apollo Maleatas would stand more than a thousand years later, three people were laid in pits on their sides, knees drawn up, under slabs of coarse limestone. Radiocarbon puts all three graves in the 19th century BCE, in the Middle Bronze Age. Ancient DNA marks two of them as first-degree relatives, probably father and daughter, and her tooth enamel carries a strontium signature foreign to the mountain while his matches the ground around it. items.abstract: CAIRO, EGYPT—Ahram Online reports that a pyramid-shaped tomb dated to the late third or early […] The post Pyramid-Shaped Tomb Unearthed in Egypt’s Dakhleh Oasis appeared first on Archaeology Magazine . CAIRO, EGYPT— Ahram Online reports that a pyramid-shaped tomb dated to the late third or early fourth century A.D. has been unearthed at the site of Bir Al-Shaghala in the Dakhleh Oasis by archaeologists from Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities. Bir Al-Shaghala was part of the necropolis of Mothis, the oasis' capital during the Ptolemaic and Roman periods. Underneath the pyramid superstructure, the researchers uncovered a mudbrick hall with a vaulted ceiling. Two mudbrick burial chambers were set to the right of the hall. The staircase and the sandstone entrance to the tomb were built in the Egyptian style, with hieroglyphic inscriptions of funerary spells and protections. A cornice decorated with a winged sun disk and two cobras, and a funerary scene from the Egyptian Books of the Netherworld on the lintel, also reflect Egyptian style. items.title: Artifacts in Etruscan Tomb Reflect Mediterranean Trade
items.abstract: ROME, ITALY—According to the Greek Reporter, an international team of researchers has uncovered a tomb […] The post Artifacts in Etruscan Tomb Reflect Mediterranean Trade appeared first on Archaeology Magazine . Etruscan tomb near Vulci, Italy ROME, ITALY—According to the Greek Reporter , an international team of researchers has uncovered a tomb dating to the late seventh century B.C. in a necropolis near the site of the Etruscan city of Vulci. The tomb had three rooms made of large blocks of volcanic stone, but repeated looting in the twentieth century caused the roof and walls to collapse. The resulting layers of rubble protected the remaining artifacts. Archaeologists from Sapienza University, the French School at Rome, and the British Museum recovered local pottery as well as ceramics imported from Athens and Corinth, ceremonial dining vessels, weapons, chariot fittings, a bronze tripod, a lamp made of gypsum alabaster, carved bone and ivory, jewelry, and women’s footwear from the tomb. Located in southeastern Turkey, the monumental structures and pillars were built by hunter-gatherers in several stages between 9600 and 8200 B.C. A kidney-shaped pit was found to contain the remains of a woman, a young man, and an adolescent girl. The remains of a young woman were found in a flexed position in a single burial. These graves have been dated to between about 8700 and 8000 B.C. The researchers now think that the bone fragments found in buildings may have been placed there during ritual activity. items.abstract: A dying Henry Dashwood is clear about his wishes. His son and heir, John, should provide for his stepmother and his three half-sisters, Elinor, Marianne and Margaret. But John’s wife, Fanny, sees things differently, which leaves the quartet facing life in greatly reduced circumstances… Published in October 1811 in an edition that credited the text only to “A Lady”, Jane Austen first began working on Sense and Sensibility at the end of the 18th century. The first draft was written in epistolary form, a style popularised by Samuel Richardson (1689–1761), a novelist she admired. The revised approach likely gave Austen more flexibility in exploring the world of the Dashwoods, and their struggles to adjust to a life where they are often reliant on the kindness and assistance of family and friends. The new version is directed by Georgia Oakley. It’s her second feature after her acclaimed Blue Jean (2022), which was set in 1988 and focused on the effects of Section 28 legislation on a lesbian teacher. items.abstract: BASEL, SWITZERLAND—SwissInfo reports that a nearly intact medieval heating system has been found at the […] The post Medieval Heating System Discovered in Switzerland appeared first on Archaeology Magazine . Flue of the heating system from the Gnadental Convent, Basel, Switzerland Green-glazed stove tile BASEL, SWITZERLAND— SwissInfo reports that a nearly intact medieval heating system has been found at the site of Gnadental Convent, which was built outside the walls of the city of Basel around 1231. The heating system consisted of an underground chamber lined with stones to hold heat produced by a firebox channel beneath it. Eight openings allowed warm air to rise from the chamber up into a common room thought to have been used as a dining hall. The monastery was dissolved after the Protestant Reformation in the sixteenth century, but some of the buildings were repurposed, or new buildings were constructed with materials from the convent. items.title: Archaeologists uncover centuries-old mystery of Tampa Bay's secret community of migrant potters
items.abstract: About 100 years ago, archaeologists unearthing pottery sherds in Tampa Bay found something unexpected. Some of the fragments they recovered had designs nearly identical to decorated pottery found hundreds of miles to the north. At least on the surface, the pottery appeared to be Mississippian, a culture that emerged more than 1,000 years ago and brought social, economic and political transformation across southeastern North America. For years, archaeologists excluded peninsular Florida from maps of its range, but the artifacts suggested a different story.

items.title: Does Tutankhamen's tomb hold his stepmother Queen Nefertiti's remains? New study offers tantalizing clues
items.abstract: When Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered over a century ago, it became an immediate worldwide sensation, revealing a wealth of treasures from ancient Egypt. In the decades that followed, the tomb was meticulously cleared, cataloged and studied, leading many to believe that KV 62, as it is officially known, had given up all its secrets. Yet long after its opening, the boy king's final resting place may still hold mysteries.

items.title: A 66-million-year-old tooth reveals T. rex was nearly as warm as a human
items.abstract: Chemical clues preserved inside fossilized T. rex teeth reveal that the dinosaur maintained a body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit, almost identical to humans. The finding provides direct evidence that the giant predator was warm-blooded, helping explain how it stayed active and survived in chilly environments as far north as Alaska.

items.title: The monsters that weren't: Dinosaur and tusked-beast claims in San rock art unravel
items.abstract: For decades, an idea has grown in paleontology that, long before scientists began digging up and reconstructing dinosaur bones, the Indigenous San and Basotho in southern Africa noticed them too, incorporating them into songs, myths and immortalizing them on cave walls. But under closer scrutiny, these claims begin to crumble.

items.title: Scientists discover the first diplodocus ever found outside North America
items.abstract: A 150-million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Spain has been identified as the first confirmed Diplodocus ever found outside North America. The giant sauropod measured about 25 meters long and was preserved well enough for researchers to match distinctive features in its tail bones to the famous genus. Its unexpected appearance in Europe suggests dinosaurs were moving between the continents during the Late Jurassic, possibly across temporary land connections.

items.title: Medieval Chinese skeleton may reveal first evidence of a brutal punishment
items.abstract: Ancient Chinese authorities used many creative ways to punish people, often with methods designed to mark them for life. One brutal example mentioned repeatedly in historical texts is cutting off a person's nose. However, archaeologists in China have never found skeletal evidence to prove that it occurred. But that may have changed following the discovery of a skeleton of a woman who lived in China about 700 years ago.

items.title: WHAT ONCE WAS SHALL BE AGAIN: PALAEOLITHIC BIFACES AT THE NEOLITHIC SITE OF GIV'AT RABI EAST
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary Giv'at Rabi East is a Pre‐Pottery Neolithic B site located in northern Israel, interpreted as a flint workshop. One area has been spatially identified as a ‘biface locality’; it is characterized by the presence of finished axes and preforms alongside débitage. Interestingly, Acheulean bifaces have also been recovered from this area. Aside from these, no other diagnostic Lower Palaeolithic artefacts have been identified, and the integrity of the Neolithic contexts is well established. It is therefore suggested that Neolithic knappers collected Acheulian bifaces from nearby sites and brought them to the workshop. Technological similarity along with an apparent appreciation for artefacts knapped hundreds of thousands of years earlier – and for the ancient people who knapped them – may partially explain this intriguing phenomenon. These findings shed new light on the enduring significance of bifacial tools in the lives of Neolithic communities in the southern Levant.

items.abstract: A 5,900-year-old Copper Age pottery kiln at Ursoaia, Romania, is larger than any kiln yet published from the Trypillia megasites. Its buried lower chamber measures 3.10 by 2.40 meters, and the grate it carried, a floor of loose clay slabs on which vessels were stacked for firing, covered roughly 7.5 square meters (about 81 square feet), a number that means little until it is set beside the kilns of the places that ought to have outbuilt it. Cucuteni-Trypillia (Cucuteni in Romanian usage, Trypillia in Ukrainian) is a Copper Age farming culture, the Chalcolithic in technical terms, that spread across what is now eastern Romania, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine. Its best-known settlements are the megasites of central Ukraine, among them Maidanetske, Talianki and Nebelivka, each covering well over a hundred hectares and ranking among the largest settlements in Europe in the early fourth millennium BCE. items.title: 8,000 Insect Remains Show a Gran Canaria Tomb Was a Granary
items.abstract: Archaeoentomology at Cruz de la Esquina shows Indigenous Canarians buried their dead fresh, on planks laid over the leftovers of stored grain. The weevil is a pest of stored cereal. Its larvae grow inside single grains, hollowing out the starchy endosperm, and in the temperate places where it thrives it ranks among the most destructive insects a grain store can have. items.abstract: About 40 years ago, researchers found ancient ship carvings on a temple wall in Cyprus, possibly all carved at once at the tail end of the Bronze Age, around the time of the infamous Bronze Age collapse. items.abstract: For many, the Bayeux Tapestry conjures images of clinker-built ships, prancing horses, the Normans feasting on chicken on the eve of the Battle of Hastings, and the arrow in King Harold's eye that ended centuries of Anglo-Saxon rule.

items.abstract: Sir John Gage, a key figure in Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries, saved a dangerous Catholic book from likely destruction, a new study suggests. The identification of six lost pages of a medieval bestseller—illicitly prized by Catholics in the Reformation—as belonging to Gage, exposes the split loyalties of one of Tudor England's great survivors.

items.abstract: Archaeologists have analyzed insect remains preserved in the 7th to 9th centuries AD funerary cave of Cruz de la Esquina, Gran Canaria, and found that it was used by the island's Indigenous people for food storage before being adapted into a burial site. The findings have been published in the journal Antiquity.

items.title: A sharper picture of a pandemic: Uncovering the complex history of the plague after the Black Death
items.abstract: The Black Death is often remembered as a single catastrophic event that swept across Europe between 1347 and 1353, killing millions. Yet the disease did not disappear after that first devastating outbreak. For more than four centuries, plague continued to return in recurring waves, reshaping communities, economies and societies across Europe and beyond. A new study led by researchers at the University of Tartu sheds fresh light on this long and complex history by analyzing the DNA of the plague bacterium preserved in archaeological human remains. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

In the Silberberg Grotto at Sterkfontein, northwest of Johannesburg, two technicians spent about two days in 1997 searching mining rubble by hand-held lamp for the spot where a shin bone had snapped. Stephen Motsumi and Nkwane Molefe carried a cast of the broken piece, which the paleoanthropologist Ronald Clarke of the University of the Witwatersrand had recognized in a box of monkey fossils. They found its match jutting from the breccia, the cemented rubble filling the cave. Behind it lay the rest of an Australopithecus skeleton, catalogued as StW 573 and nicknamed Little Foot for four small foot bones Clarke had noticed in 1994. Freeing it took more than a decade, and the sediment that held it has been dated to about 3.67 million years ago. Anyone who learned human origins through Lucy probably holds a tidy picture of her genus. items.abstract: Seeds from Phoenician-era Huelva and Islamic Valencia put some Iberian wine grapes two or three generations from vines that reached Spain 3,000 years ago. At Finca La Grajera, on the edge of Logroño, the Institute of Grapevine and Wine Sciences (ICVV) keeps a collection of grape varieties 410 meters above sea level, and one of them is an old Spanish cultivar called Heben. Its vines are trained along two cordon arms, pruned back to short spurs, and grafted, as most European vines have been since phylloxera, onto a rootstock known as R-110. For a new study, researchers picked young Heben leaves and sequenced the genome to more than 70-fold depth, because they needed a clean modern genome to set beside something much older. The older thing was a grape seed from Valencia, recovered below the water table in the moat of the city’s Islamic wall and dated by its deposits to the tenth century CE. Ancient DNA in grape seeds comes mostly from the seed coat, which is maternal tissue, so what the team sequenced was in effect the genome of the vine that bore the seed. items.abstract: At Mizyn in northern Ukraine, Ice Age carvers engraved the Schreger lines of mammoth ivory onto some of Europe’s earliest schematic female figurines. Sometime in 1912 or 1913, excavators at Mizyn, a village on the Desna River in northern Ukraine, found three small ivory carvings of the kind usually called Venus figurines lying beneath a mammoth skull, or possibly inside it; the records are too thin to say which. The skull belonged to one of the site’s circular settings of mammoth bone, generally read as the remains of dwellings, and the carvings were themselves mammoth ivory, so whoever left them there put pieces of a mammoth back with a mammoth. A study published September 11 in npj Heritage Science 1 2 argues that the carvers had already worked the tusk itself into their designs. Mizyn, which older literature often spells Mezin, has yielded 18 of these figurines, the largest group of female figures from Eastern Europe after the Last Glacial Maximum, the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age. items.title: Ancient DNA: Coastal and Inland Finns Were One People in 1250
items.abstract: Genomes from 34 Iron Age and medieval burials show how Swedish migration after 1250 reshaped Finland’s southwest coast while inland Häme barely changed. Sometime between 1031 and 1147, a woman was buried at Laukskola, a cemetery on the Daugava River in Latvia. Her community probably spoke Liv, a Finnic language that has nearly died out, and its grave goods are rich enough that archaeologists tie its wealth to the trading places along the river. Her genome, already published, turns up in a new analysis with long stretches of DNA that match two people buried in Finland in roughly the same period. One was buried at Raisio, on the edge of Turku near the southwest coast. The other was a parent buried at Mikkola, in the inland municipality of Ylöjärvi, at the same site as three of that parent’s children. The amount of DNA involved puts both relationships at sixth cousins or more distant, implying an ancestor some generations back who crossed between Latvia and southwestern Finland in one direction or the other. items.abstract: A newly identified 240-million-year-old animal from Tanzania is forcing scientists to rethink the early dinosaur timeline. Dinodontosaurus isiyavamanda belongs to a group previously known only from South America, linking fossil deposits on the two continents. That connection suggests Tanzania’s supposed oldest dinosaur fossils may actually be millions of years younger than previously thought.

items.title: FROM SCANDINAVIA TO THE LEVANT: THE LATE BRONZE AGE METAL TRADE AND NURAGIC SARDINIA
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary A growing body of evidence suggests that Nuragic Sardinia played a role, as yet poorly understood, in the metal trade between Scandinavia, Atlantic Europe, and the Mediterranean during the Bronze Age. Provenance studies based on lead isotope and chemical analyses of copper‐based – and to a minor extent lead – artefacts from both continental Europe and the Mediterranean indicate that metals of Sardinian origin were exported and used in different and far apart regions over the second half of the second millennium BC. This noticeable flow of metals from Sardinia appears associated to distinct counter‐flows of Nuragic pottery both to the east and to the west of the island. Breaking down the chronology of such movements unveils specific distribution patterns over different phases of the Bronze Age. By critically assessing such patterns, this paper discusses how the study of Nuragic Sardinia may contribute to a refined understanding of the complex interplay between the socio‐political transformations that characterize Bronze Age Europe and what must have been a permanent demand for metal.

items.title: MINDING THE GAP: A METHODOLOGICAL AND CHRONOLOGICAL REASSESSMENT OF EASTERN MEDITERRANEAN PURPLE‐DYE PRODUCTION IN THE BRONZE AND IRON AGES
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary Purple dye was an iconic status symbol in the ancient Mediterranean, yet tracing the expansion and shift of production from the Aegean to the Levant encounters substantial methodological difficulties. Using Tel Shiqmona – a unique industrial centre with a continuous Iron Age sequence – as an archaeological benchmark, this study defines detailed and granular criteria for identifying production. Applying these criteria reveals a 300‐year ‘gap’ (c.950–650 BC), when Shiqmona remains the sole site with significant production evidence. This paper argues the gap represents a consolidation: a shift from dispersed crafts into centralized, state‐controlled production, first attested at Shiqmona in the ninth century BC. By providing a chronologically sensitive database for the Levant, this study lays foundations for examining broader Mediterranean‐wide trajectories. The centralized and specialized production attested at Shiqmona offers a plausible template for understanding the industry’s seventh century BC resurgence in the Levant, as the wider adoption of the ‘Shiqmona model’ under Neo‐Assyrian hegemony.

items.title: MIDDLE IRON AGE V‐SHAPED PRECIOUS METAL FINGER‐RINGS IN BRITAIN
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary The first V‐shaped finger‐ring reported from Britain was a silver specimen found in 1921–26. No more came to light until discoveries of gold examples by metal detectorists from 1997 onwards. There are now ten such gold rings from Britain, a third of the European total. There is no trail of these gold rings known between their Central European homeland and the English Channel, making those in Britain a distinctly anomalous phenomenon. They first appear c.400 BC in Austria‐Slovakia. Their popularity peaked at the end of the fourth and in the early third centuries BC. Afterwards, there was a steep decline, and they were not made at all later than c.200 BC. Although none from Britain has a context or definite associations, they can be proposed as ritual offerings of jewellery worn by elite women. Their currency in Britain spanned the period between the first arrivals of continental gold torcs and the development of insular schools of gold jewellery.

items.title: 324-million-year-old fossil reveals how insects conquered land
items.abstract: Ancient fossils suggest insects conquered land through a long amphibious phase rather than making an abrupt jump from water to dry ground. A newly identified 324-million-year-old species still carried paddle-like abdominal limbs, revealing an evolutionary bridge between aquatic ancestors and modern six-legged insects.

items.title: Archaeologists discover mysterious 400-year-old Indigenous pot in Florida
items.abstract: A tiny, fully intact Indigenous pot buried for roughly 400 years has left archaeologists wondering why such a usable object was deliberately abandoned. Found at a historic Potano-Timucua village in Florida, the mysterious vessel is helping reveal a complex world of Native traditions, Spanish influence, trade, and migration.

items.abstract: For generations, researching family history has meant searching through dusty archives, reading handwritten documents, studying old photographs, and piecing together fragmented stories. Today, artificial intelligence is beginning to change that process. Modern AI genealogy tools, including platforms such as Vestigee, can help people explore family records, identify potential connections, restore historical photographs, and turn static ... items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
items.abstract: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
items.abstract: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

items.title: When an American Airplane Crashed Into a School in 1944, an English Village Lost Almost All of Its Youngest Children. Why Has WWII's Worst Civilian Aviation Accident Been Forgotten?
items.abstract: On August 23, 1944, a test flight over the village of Freckleton, located in northwest England, ended in disaster, claiming the lives of 61 people, including 38 students between the ages of 4 and 6

items.title: Is Türkiye’s Megalithic Archaeological Site Göbeklitepe a Temple?
items.abstract: While shooting a documentary at Göbeklitepe, I encountered strikingly different historical interpretations of the site. An international group of New Age seekers seemed to be searching for extraterrestrial connections there, but when I pointed out that the enclosures had originally been roofed, they recast the T-shaped pillars as traces of humanity’s mystical past. Representatives of an NGO ... Read more »

items.title: This 23-foot crocodylian may have ruled South America’s food chain
items.abstract: Miocene South America was packed with giant prey—and the predators hunting them were just as spectacular. Fossil bite marks suggest crocodylians, especially the enormous Purussaurus neivensis, were more important predators than mammals in this ancient tropical ecosystem. At around seven meters long, Purussaurus may even have helped control populations of giant herbivores.

items.title: 16 mummies and a dog reveal a hidden order inside an ancient Egyptian tomb
items.abstract: A tomb in Egypt’s Theban Necropolis reveals a surprisingly organized story of burial, reuse, and changing beliefs spanning hundreds of years. Researchers found 16 mummified people, the remains of at least four more, and a mummified dog, with burials ranging from wealthy individuals laid in coffins with amulets and imported goods to later bodies carefully stacked in increasingly crowded spaces.

items.title: Tiny 1.7-billion-year-old fossils could reveal how complex life began
items.abstract: Scientists are searching some of Earth’s oldest rocks for tiny fossils that could reveal how simple microbial life made the extraordinary leap toward plants, animals, and other complex organisms. Solving that ancient mystery may also help determine whether complex life could emerge on worlds beyond Earth.

items.title: Olga Soffer obituary
items.abstract: Professor of anthropology whose approach to archaeology centred on crafts executed by women 40,000 years ago Olga Soffer, who has died aged 83, brought a revolutionary idea into the conversation about prehistoric ice age people: women mattered. Inspired when working on archaeological excavations in the former USSR, and by remains from a dig in Moravia, in the 1990s she presented a case for women as makers of textiles, baskets and nets, critical to survival in bleak northern conditions 30,000 years ago. Her achievement was the more remarkable for her career path. By then a professor of anthropology at the University of Illinois, she had obtained her three degrees over three decades, partly while also working as a cosmetics buyer and fashion promoter for a New York department store. Continue reading...

items.title: Block export of ‘national treasure’ UK fossils, says MP
items.abstract: Sale of one of UK’s top collections overseas prompts call new rules to help keep items in country One of UK’s best fossil collections sold in ‘loss to the nation’ An MP has called on ministers to change export controls so that significant fossils can be classed as national treasures after one of the UK’s best collections, unearthed on Dorset beaches, was sold overseas. Last week, a Guardian investigation revealed that an unparalleled collection of fossils from the UK’s Jurassic Coast, comprising hundreds of specimens including ichthyosaurs, had been sold to the Natural History Museum in Abu Dhabi for what one source described as an “eight-figure sum”. Continue reading...

items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
items.abstract: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

items.title: 3,500-year-old skeletons challenge what scientists thought they knew about syphilis
items.abstract: Ancient remains from Vietnam suggest diseases like yaws may have been passed from mother to child thousands of years ago, a form of transmission often assumed to indicate syphilis. The discovery could overturn how scientists interpret ancient infections and complicate the long-running mystery of syphilis’s origins.

items.title: Scientists find evidence for two origins of life on Earth
items.abstract: Scientists probing life’s deepest origins have uncovered evidence that the first free-living cells may have emerged not once, but twice. The findings suggest a striking possibility: life may share one ancient genetic code, yet have undergone two separate transitions into free-living existence.

items.title: ‘Real mummy’s curse’: health warning over growing trade in mummified human remains
items.abstract: Academic paper says often illicit trade exposes enthusiasts – and postal workers handling items – to serious risks A growing global trade in mummified human remains has been described by academics as “a real mummy’s curse” that poses a serious health risk to its enthusiasts and the postal services they use. Research into the secretive buying and selling of centuries-old human body parts including hands, feet and heads found alarming risks from dormant microorganisms and the toxic materials used to preserve the remains. Continue reading...

items.title: King Harold may have lost England by backing the wrong pope
items.abstract: A forgotten fragment of a lost papal letter is offering a surprising new explanation for the Norman Conquest. England may have backed the wrong pope during a bitter religious power struggle, giving Pope Alexander II a political reason to support William the Conqueror’s invasion. The discovery suggests Harold’s downfall in 1066 was shaped by intrigue in Rome as well as bloodshed at Hastings.

items.title: The secret hidden in these ancient manuscripts isn’t written in ink
items.abstract: Researchers can now recover DNA from centuries-old parchment without damaging the manuscripts, turning historic documents into unexpected genetic time capsules. The hidden clues could reveal ancient trade routes, livestock history, manuscript origins, and details of everyday life stretching back more than a thousand years.

items.abstract: Nobody knows who dropped Speedy Weber's correspondence at a USO office in 2022. Researchers have finally tracked down two living relatives who remember him

items.title: 240-million-year-old reptile fossil reveals a lost chapter before dinosaurs and crocodiles
items.abstract: A 240-million-year-old reptile discovered in Brazil is revealing what evolution looked like just before the rise of dinosaurs and crocodiles. The small predator had unusually positioned legs that may have allowed it to move more efficiently than many earlier reptiles. Its close relatives were previously known mostly from other continents, suggesting these ancient animals spread much farther across the Triassic world than scientists realized.

items.title: Roman shipwreck with 500 amphorae found off coast of Sicily
items.abstract: Discovery of 2,100-year-old vessel hailed as ‘one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years’ A 2,100-year-old Roman shipwreck carrying about 500 amphorae has been discovered 3 miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo in Sicily. Italy’s Carabinieri cultural heritage protection squad investigated the wreck with the help of divers and underwater cameras after receiving a tip-off from fishers. The vessel was found at a depth of about 46 metres (151ft) and was carrying hundreds of amphorae – ancient two-handled ceramic jars with a narrow neck – thought to have been used mainly to transport wine. Continue reading...

items.abstract: Italy's Carabinieri cultural protection unit has discovered the wreck of a Roman ship off Sicily. Divers found hundreds of amphorae and parts of anchors inside the vessel, which was located about 3 miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo. Sicily, colonised by the ancient Greeks from around the eighth century BC, and conquered by the Romans in about 240BC, was an important centre of trade in the ancient world Continue reading...

items.title: For 15,000 years, humans and dogs have been changing each other
items.abstract: Dogs have been shaping—and being shaped by—humans for about 15,000 years, evolving from early partners of hunter-gatherers into an astonishing range of specialized companions. Across the globe, they adapted alongside people to wildly different environments and needs, from powerful Arctic sled dogs and agile rainforest hunters to high-altitude dogs with genetic traits for surviving thin air. Some were even bred for wool, while others played important spiritual or ceremonial roles.

items.title: Dinosaurs became giants — so why did they never become tiny?
items.abstract: Dinosaurs conquered the land at enormous sizes, but strangely, they almost never evolved into truly tiny animals. New research suggests that physiology alone can’t explain this missing miniature end of the dinosaur spectrum—and that early mammals may have been partly responsible. While dinosaurs kept mammals from becoming large, small mammals may have returned the favor by occupying ecological niches that could otherwise have supported mouse-sized dinosaurs.

items.title: Scientists find unexpected life on Ötzi the Iceman’s 5,300-year-old body
items.abstract: More than 5,000 years after his death, Ötzi the Iceman is still hosting a remarkable mix of ancient and modern microorganisms. Researchers separated microbes that lived in his body during his lifetime from those that arrived after his death, uncovering traces of his original gut bacteria and cold-loving yeasts that may have survived alongside him in the glacier for millennia.

items.abstract: A spectacular fossil site in Canada contains 567-million-year-old creatures that may represent some of the earliest animals to move, reproduce sexually, and develop recognizable body plans. The discovery pushes key evolutionary milestones back by up to 10 million years and suggests complex animal life may have first flourished in the deep ocean.

items.title: 80-million-year-old snake brain reveals a surprising evolutionary secret
items.abstract: An exceptionally preserved snake fossil from Brazil reveals that early snakes were far more diverse than scientists once thought. Detailed brain reconstructions show that Tametara mirim was adapted for burrowing, while another ancient snake was suited to life above ground. Other fossils point to marine lifestyles as well. By 80 million years ago, snakes were already experimenting with very different habitats and sensory systems.

items.title: This school-bus-sized “terror croc” ate dinosaurs. Now it’s back
items.abstract: A massive crocodilian capable of attacking dinosaurs has been brought back to life as the first scientifically accurate mounted skeleton of Deinosuchus schwimmeri. The 31-foot replica at Georgia’s Tellus Science Museum was built from detailed fossil scans and more than 40 years of research by paleontologist Dr. David Schwimmer, for whom the species was named.

items.title: 518-million-year-old creature reveals the origins of spider fangs
items.abstract: A tiny 518-million-year-old sea creature has revealed the earliest known evidence of the structures that eventually became spiders’ fangs. Hidden inside the fossil were pincerlike limbs and preserved soft tissues that help explain how the ancestors of spiders and scorpions evolved into formidable hunters.

items.title: Scientists found two mysterious ‘ghost’ ancestors hiding in our DNA
items.abstract: Modern humans carry DNA from two mysterious extinct lineages in addition to Neanderthals and Denisovans. Their hidden genetic legacy shows that our evolutionary past was shaped by repeated mixing among many different human groups.

items.title: This 4,000-year-old city defied the rules of history
items.abstract: As Mohenjo-daro prospered, the gap between its richest and poorest households actually shrank. Its shared infrastructure, fair trade systems, and lack of powerful royal elites suggest that equality may have helped fuel the ancient city’s success.

items.title: A forgotten fossil just revealed a new Triassic predator from 210 million years ago
items.abstract: A fossil overlooked for nearly 80 years has revealed a previously unknown crocodile relative that lived 210 million years ago in what is now New Mexico. Named Eosphorosuchus lacrimosa, the jackal-sized predator had a reinforced skull, powerful jaw muscles, and a short snout built for tackling larger prey.

items.title: Magic circle: Stonehenge offers lucky visitors 20 minutes alone in monument
items.abstract: Handful of ticketholders will be selected at random for up-close visits to ancient site throughout August Trips to Stonehenge can be a little hectic. Tens of thousands of people turn up to celebrate summer and winter solstices and most other days the site is a place of bustle, excited conversation and selfie action. But throughout August, English Heritage is offering visitors the chance to win some guaranteed solitude within the hulking stones. Continue reading...

items.title: Hidden charcoal reveals the true age of ancient cave paintings
items.abstract: A new analysis has precisely dated paintings in France’s Font-de-Gaume cave for the first time. Scientists discovered charcoal inside black pigments once thought to contain only minerals, allowing them to use radiocarbon dating. The results show that a bison was painted about 13,000 years ago, while sections of a mask-like figure were added during several widely separated periods.

items.title: The Guardian view on ancient DNA: a female shaman exposes our flawed assumptions about the past | Editorial
items.abstract: Thanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly know Archaeologists believe the Upton Lovell Shaman, who lived in what is now Wiltshire 4,000 years ago, was an important religious leader and metalworker because of the artefacts and tools buried with the body. Until very recently it was also believed, on considerably slimmer evidence, that this shaman was a man: it was simply assumed that someone of such status must be male, and the view was barely questioned over the years. Now ancient DNA analysis performed at the Francis Crick Institute has revealed that the body, held by the Wiltshire Museum, is in fact a woman. That should cause a stir in bronze-age studies. But it is also yet another example of how many of our assumptions about human history have been upended by the rise of ancient DNA analysis over the past two decades. Others include the revelation that there were (frequent) liaisons between humans and Neanderthals just 50,000 years ago, a reconstruction suggesting that the first modern Britons had “dark to black” skin, and the closing of longstanding mysteries such as what really killed two members …

items.title: 500,000-year-old elephant bone hammer shows ancient humans were master toolmakers
items.abstract: Early humans in England crafted a rare piece of elephant bone into a reusable hammer for sharpening stone tools nearly 500,000 years ago. The extraordinary find reveals that ancient toolmakers were resourceful, skilled, and capable of surprisingly advanced planning.

items.abstract: Jewellery with origins in Iran worn at an Odyssey photocall turns the spotlight on the trade in archaeological finds The Odyssey has stormed cinemas, but while its take on the Homeric epic has created ripples among western classicists, it is an actor’s earrings that have made waves further afield. Zendaya, who portrays the goddess Athena in the movie, provoked outrage when she appeared at a London photocall wearing earrings that were allegedly made from Iranian artefacts dating back to the 1st millennium BC. Continue reading...

items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt challenges the story of human origins
items.abstract: A newly identified fossil ape from northern Egypt is reshaping ideas about where the ancestors of modern apes first emerged. Analyses place it closer to living apes than any known East African species of the same age, pointing to North Africa and the Middle East as a possible birthplace and crossroads for the ape lineage that eventually produced gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

items.title: New giant salamander species discovered in 3.5-million-year-old fossils
items.abstract: Fossils discovered in Japan more than two decades ago have finally been identified as a new genus and species of giant salamander. Limnospondylus ajimuensis lived around 3.5 million years ago in a warmer, wetter Kyushu and may have reached 1.1 meters in length. Its discovery hints that many more unknown giant salamanders could be hiding among fossils previously given the wrong classification.

items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 330-348, August 2026. Summary During the Bronze Age, a particular type of podomorphic petroglyph was produced on the outcrops by the sea in southern Scandinavia. In this text, their distribution, organization and articulation are analyzed in the Mälaren region of central‐eastern Sweden. The study shows that the petroglyphs are organized in relation to water as well as to different minerals visible in the rock. This pattern indicates that they are not simply images or symbols but also physical ‘devices’, produced to do something. It is argued that one purpose was for the frequent single podomorphs to be paired with another at a later stage. Because podomorphs in a pair generally are of different sizes and form, it is suggested that each one belongs to an individual of different age and/or sex – potentially depicted in stone to show existing or desired future relations, agreements, pacts, friendship, marriages etc.

Summary This article analyses the dynamics of Roman olive‐oil and wine production and commerce in present‐day France from the second half of the second century BC to the mid‐fourth century AD, drawing on a corpus of more than 7000 amphorae recovered from Gallic and Romano‐Gallic settlements across the French territory, excluding Alsace. The methodology consists of a quantitative strategy based on aoristic distribution, assessing both regional and chronological trends according to production and settlement chronologies. The results highlight a clear preponderance of Italic wine in Late Republican Gaul, followed by imports from Hispania, before local Gallic wine came to dominate the domestic market and expanded to other provincial contexts. In parallel, the study traces initial Italic olive‐oil imports to southern Gaul, subsequently supplanted by the predominance of Hispanic oil and the growing presence of North African products. The article follows these dynamics up to the mid‐fourth century AD, considering both the impact of the crisis of the third century and the substitution of amphorae by barrels in no…

items.title: OLD SEALS NEW STORIES: THE COPPER AGE–EARLY BRONZE AGE STONE STAMP SEALS AND SEALING PRACTICES FROM ALİŞAR HÖYÜK
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 306-329, August 2026. Summary This study examines 13 stone stamp seals excavated from the Copper and Early Bronze Age levels at Alişar and currently housed in the Museum of Anatolian Civilisations at Ankara (Türkiye). Through detailed documentation, typological analysis and comparison with sealing traditions in Anatolia and neighbouring regions, it explores their formal, iconographic and cultural characteristics. The seals demonstrate transcultural distribution patterns, reflecting intensified interregional interactions in the latter half of the Early Bronze Age. In particular, serpentine seals – similar in form to metal examples – are thought to have been burnished and used as alternatives to metal ones. It is also suggested that these stone seals may have been produced by local artisans. The Alişar seal assemblage reveals a synthesis of local and external influences and likely fulfilled both administrative and symbolic functions. By systematically presenting the typological diversity of the Alişar seals, this study sheds light on the cultural dynamics and interregional connections of Anatolia during the Early Bronze Age.

items.title: BRINGING BACK FAMILIAR FORMS: RECYCLING QUINA SCRAPERS AT THE LATE LOWER PALAEOLITHIC QESEM CAVE, ISRAEL
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 250-277, August 2026. Summary This study presents a technological analysis of 18 old patinated scrapers and spalls, mostly of Quina technology, that were recycled into new scrapers of the same type at the Late Lower Palaeolithic site of Qesem Cave, Israel (420–200 kyr). Recycling scrapers into the same Quina and demi‐Quina types offers a rare, controlled opportunity to investigate a technology’s biographical character. Comparing the tools’ pre‐ and post‐recycling phases demonstrates that the selection of old items was highly intentional, guided by the original tool’s morphology and the affordances of its pre‐existing features. This process suggests an enacted perceptual experience, demonstrating a skilled recognition of the potential remaining in discarded objects. A sophisticated understanding of material properties and technological trajectories is thus revealed. This behaviour suggests a form of historically‐aware material engagement, offering new insights into the cognitive and technological capabilities of Late Lower Palaeolithic humans and providing a basis for future cognitive studies.

items.title: ARROWHEAD OR SPEARPOINT? EXPERIMENTAL ANALYSIS OF IMPACT TRACES ON SLOTTED BONE POINTS WITH MICROBLADE INSETS
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 278-305, August 2026. Summary Slotted bone points likely originated in Palaeolithic traditions and evolved into efficient, reusable Mesolithic hunting weapons optimized for reliability and increased bleeding, reducing the risk of hunting failure. Such bone points were long debated as either spear tips or arrowheads, but earlier interpretations lacked reliable criteria. A newly conducted experiment show they function effectively as arrowheads when mounted on appropriate shafts and fired with bows of realistic Mesolithic draw weight. Damage patterns on bone points and insets matches archaeological finds from Motala in south‐central Sweden. Microblade durability varied with the inset raw material, though penetration did not. The type of adhesive had minimal effect on performance. The design’s main advantage lies in its long cutting edges, which create larger wound channels than plain bone points.

items.title: CONNECTIVITY AND CHANGE: GLAZED POTTERY NETWORKS IN THE MEDIEVAL EASTERN MEDITERRANEAN (ELEVENTH–FOURTEENTH CENTURIES AD)
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 369-393, August 2026. Summary This paper investigates the economic and political transformations of the Medieval Eastern Mediterranean (late eleventh to mid‐fourteenth centuries AD) through the lens of material culture and Social Network Analysis (SNA). Using the distribution of seven types of glazed pottery as archaeological indicators, the study examines changing patterns of connectivity and the structural positions of sites within regional exchange systems. By applying SNA to presence/absence datasets, the analysis reconstructs the topology of interaction networks revealing a shift from a Byzantine‐centred system to one increasingly shaped by Italian maritime powers and the Crusader States, with the events of 1204 marking a critical turning point. Interpreted within a world‐systems perspective, the results trace the relocation of core functions from Byzantine centres to Italian city‐states, while highlighting the resilience of long‐established hubs within the reconfigured system.
